name: Serua
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Only Taber 1993 survey and Edwards 2021 classification named on Glottolog; no descriptive source for Serua located

sources.citation: Grimes, Charles E. & Owen Edwards. 2026. The Austronesian languages of eastern Indonesia and Timor-Leste: Unravelling their prehistory and classification. Berlin: Language Science Press (langsci 526; Zenodo 18323007).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Sec. 4.6.4 Teun-Nila-Serua (pp. 217-223) is historical phonology only (Serua *z>s, *ay>i, *b>w, loss of initial *w, *ŋ>n/zero, *d/*j/*R>r), Lesluru data; no synchronic stress statement for Serua. Only a generic areal remark p. 115: 'penultimate stress is the normal rule for Wallacean languages'. Notes (p. 540 fn) that Taber 1993 transcribes stress marks in his wordlists.

sources.citation: Edwards, Owen. 2025. Teun, Nila, Serua (Indonesia) - A collection of language snapshots. Language Documentation and Description 25(1): 1-12. DOI 10.25894/ldd.2615
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing (sociolinguistic snapshot: history, vitality, speaker counts). Valuable 'Previous research' section listing every Serua source: Taber 1993 wordlist; van Engelenhoven 2003, 2010; Chlenov & Chlenova 2004 grammatical notes; Chlenova 2004 521-item wordlist; Hasan et al. 2021 61-page Serua-Indonesian dictionary (Kantor Bahasa Maluku); unpublished Collins 1991, Workala 1993, Workala 2017; Edwards 2023 ELAR 505-item wordlist + texts.

sources.citation: van Engelenhoven, Aone. 2009 [cited as 2010]. Change, oblivion and death: three stages in language endangerment. CenPRIS Working Paper 133. hdl 1887/15963
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing; sec. 3 'Language erosion: Serua' treats loss of possessive suffixes and subject agreement only.

sources.citation: van Engelenhoven, Aone. 2003. Language endangerment in Indonesia: The incipient obsolescence and acute death of Teun, Nila and Serua (Central and Southwest Maluku). In M. Janse & S. Tol (eds.), Language Death and Language Maintenance, 49-80. Amsterdam: Benjamins. DOI 10.1075/cilt.240.05eng (Leiden repository scan via CORE 526344276)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 3 'Typology' (pp. 52-54) gives the Serua phoneme inventory ('relatively simple.. No instances of geminate vowels or consonants'), plural -rV with vowel copy, word- and phrase-level metathesis/apocope, possessive and agreement paradigms; no statement on stress or accent anywhere in the 33 pages (scanned a full-text search for stress/accent/syllable/penult/prosod/tone).

sources.citation: Collins, James T. 1982. Prothesis in the languages of Central Maluku: an argument from Proto-Austronesian grammar. In Halim, Carrington & Wurm (eds.), Papers from 3ICAL vol. 2 (Pacific Linguistics C-75), 187-200.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on Serua stress; Serua mentioned only as the place a shipwreck text was recorded.

sources.citation: Chlenov, Mikhail A. & Svetlana F. Chlenova. 2004 [Glottolog 2000]. Serua, a vanishing language in Eastern Indonesia. In Alieva, Dorofeeva & Sikorsky (eds.), Malay-Indonesian Studies XVI (in memory of B. B. Parnikel), 265-280/299. Moscow: Nusantara Society.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: The only grammar sketch of Serua (Glottolog listed by Glottolog as a grammar sketch, English, ~35 pp, based on Chlenov's 1960s-70s fieldwork); the Chlenovs routinely mark and describe stress in their SW Maluku sketches (West Damar, Daweloor), so this is the most likely place for an explicit Serua stress rule.

sources.citation: Collins, James T. 1991. Towards a description and classification of the language of Serua. Paper, 6th International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics, Honolulu (unpublished); also Workala, Mozes. 1993. Serua-taal-bundel (Leiden ms.) / Workala 2017 De geschiedenis van het eiland Serua (Pumbo.nl), final chapter.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Collins' 1977-79 Letwaru data are the most conservative Serua record and his paper is explicitly descriptive; Workala's learner's sketch is the only community grammar. Either may state stress; neither was accessible even to Edwards (2025).

sources.citation: Edwards, Owen. 2023. Emplawas and languages of the Babar islands (ELAR deposit IPF0417): Serua 505-item wordlist + recorded texts, Lesluru village.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: no other copy located; the linked copy was not accessible when a reader tried
sources.note: Modern phonetically transcribed wordlist with audio by a phonologist; would allow first-hand verification of Serua stress (and of Nila/Teun). Access level O but requires ELAR login.

sources.citation: Hasan, Nita Handayani, Wahyudi Pasapan, Masnita Panjaitan & Indrayadi. 2021. Kamus dwibahasa Serua-Indonesia. Ambon: Kantor Bahasa Provinsi Maluku (61 pp.).
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Government bilingual dictionary; Balai/Kantor Bahasa dictionaries often open with a brief 'ejaan dan bunyi' section that may state tekanan (stress). Ministry repository (repositori.kemendikdasmen.go.id) was unreachable during this search.

sources.citation: Chlenova, Svetlana F. 2004. The Serua wordlist [Словарь языка серуа]. Malay-Indonesian Studies XVI, 281-299. Moscow.

sources.note: 521-item Serua wordlist; if transcribed with the Chlenovs' stress apostrophe/acute it fixes stress position lexically even without a prose rule.

sources.citation: Taber, Mark. 1993. Toward a better understanding of the indigenous languages of Southwestern Maluku. Oceanic Linguistics 32(2): 389-441.

sources.note: 193-item phonetic Serua (and Nila, Teun) wordlists; Taber's transcriptions carry IPA stress marks (Grimes & Edwards 2026: 540), so stress placement can be read directly from ~190 Serua forms.
